chapters.title: Prospection
chapters.hook: I once let a bright little movie of Friday run my whole week, and it skipped the hard parts.
chapters.counterintuition: A clear future can feel like evidence. In fact, the clearer it feels, the more you need to ask what memory left out.
chapters.tryThisNow: During your next conversation about a plan, say "Before I promise I want to count one missing detail" and tally it.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Use prospection, but doubt its shine: your mind builds tomorrow from yesterday's scraps, so count missing facts before a clear forecast steers a real choice.

breakdown.fastRead:
Eden hears a rail worker in Cavendish say Phineas Gage sounds present, yet somehow gone. John Martyn Harlow can see the strange split in front of him: speech, movement, and basic sense remain, but long-range control has been hurt. The old belief says planning is just good sense plus effort. The injury says your brain has equipment for steering toward later consequences.

Prospection is the mind's way of trying tomorrow on early. You picture a later state, then let that picture guide what you do now. This gift lets you save, apologize, pack, study, and say no before trouble arrives. A clear inner movie can still be a bad map. The skill is to use the picture, then count what it may have missed.
breakdown.deepRead:
Henry Molaison sits with a test card while Hubert prepares the next question. The task looks simple from the outside: remember this, then say what comes next. After his 1953 bilateral medial temporal lobe surgery, though, ordinary new episodic memory was badly damaged. Brenda Milner's work with him helped show a hard truth. The future is not built from nothing. It borrows pieces from memory.

That is why prospection feels so personal. When you picture next winter, a tense phone call, or a new job, your mind pulls old rooms, old voices, old moods, and old endings into one fresh scene. The scene may feel made for tomorrow, but many of its parts came from yesterday. Foresight needs brakes as much as it needs pictures.

This matters when the future feels vivid enough to bully you. Cassidy may picture a smooth reply in a long text thread and promise more than she can give. The image has color and a voice, but it may leave out fatigue, a buried message, or the awkward pause when the other person asks for a date. The cost is modern and small until it is not: the reply you meant to send never goes, and the relationship cools.

Prospection is still useful. Rough pictures beat no pictures when you are making plans. The danger starts when vividness gets mistaken for proof. If the scene in your head leaves out time, friction, or other people's needs, it can feel true while pointing you wrong.
breakdown.fullRead:
A western scrub jay at Cambridge does not explain itself. It caches food, returns later, and gives Nicola Clayton a clean behavioral question: does the bird use what, where, and when, or is it only repeating a habit? The answer matters because it keeps the human story precise. Future-oriented behavior can be tested by what an animal can use, not by what we imagine it feels.

That precision helps you with your own mind. You do not need to prove that a forecast is deep or special before you inspect it. Ask what the picture is using. Is it using a real memory, a wish, a fear, a mood from the room, or a borrowed story from someone else? If you cannot tell, slow down before you let the forecast write a promise.

Phineas Gage gives the body of the problem. A tamping iron in 1848 did not make planning into a moral sermon. It made planning physical. Harlow's reports became famous because a person could remain awake and articulate while the machinery for restraint and future control was altered. When your forecast is weak, scolding yourself may miss the target. You may need better supports around the forecast: a pause, a second view, a written count of what is missing.

Henry Molaison gives the memory side. If detailed personal futures draw from detailed personal pasts, then a thin memory bank narrows what tomorrow can look like. Even without brain injury, you can see the everyday version. After one bad meeting, every future meeting may borrow the same stale ending. After one easy trip, every trip may look easy until the flight delay, the tired child, or the lost charger enters the picture.

The scrub-jays add a test. The useful question is not whether a future picture feels alive. Ask what information it carries. What is in the scene? Where does it happen? When will conditions change? A forecast earns trust when the world gets a vote.

This early lesson matters because later choices rest on this engine. You cannot stop simulating the future, and you should not try. Without prospection, you would live too close to the present. You would answer the nearest buzz, accept the nearest invitation, and forget the later version of yourself who has to pay.

The precondition is outside evidence. Prospection quietly assumes that the mind can check its private scene against facts, bodies, calendars, and other people. When that is absent, the forecast becomes a little theater with no fire exit. It may be bright. It may be fluent. It may still leave you walking into the meeting without the one thing you needed.

examples.title: Cavendish Split
examples.scenario: "He knows the words," someone says near the door, and Eden's pencil hovers over John Martyn Harlow's notes. In Cavendish, Vermont, the tamping iron has already made Phineas Gage famous in the worst way. The room holds a man who can speak, move, and answer, while the future-facing part of his conduct seems newly fragile.
examples.whatToDo: Eden records the split instead of calling it laziness. She marks speech and basic sense apart from restraint, planning, and the ability to live by later consequences.
examples.whyItMatters: The scene keeps planning physical. When you fail to steer toward tomorrow, the answer is not always a sterner speech to yourself.

examples.title: Molaison Question
examples.scenario: "Ask him about tomorrow, not only yesterday," Hubert says, and Bernard turns back to Henry Molaison at the test table. Brenda Milner's materials sit between them, but the tension is in the answer they are about to hear. After the 1953 bilateral medial temporal lobe surgery, a future lunch may be hard to picture because new memory itself is broken.
examples.whatToDo: Hubert keeps the question personal and concrete. He asks for a later scene, then listens for the detail that would normally come from remembered places and events.
examples.whyItMatters: You can stop treating imagination as a magic screen. Even new futures need old material, so thin memory can make tomorrow thin too.

examples.title: Cache Correction
examples.scenario: The fresh waxworms sit beside the dry peanuts on the Cambridge aviary tray, and trainer Russell has written "habit" too soon. In Nicola Clayton's room, the western scrub jays are not only returning to a place. Russell catches his own error when the timing cue matters. What, where, and when have to travel together.
examples.whatToDo: Russell crosses out the shortcut and rewrites the observation around the full pattern. He tracks item, place, and timing before naming the behavior.
examples.whyItMatters: The correction keeps the evidence honest. A future-looking act needs more than motion toward a familiar spot; it needs usable information.

examples.title: Unexpected Memo
examples.scenario: Brenda Milner slides the session folder across the file-room counter, and clinic assistant Agathe realizes the memo is hers to draft before Henry Molaison arrives. She writes: "Do not stop at recall. Ask for a later errand, a visitor, a meal. Note whether the scene has place and sequence. The 1953 surgery damaged new episodic memory; the future question may show what memory supplies."
examples.whatToDo: Agathe turns the plan into exact prompts. She writes questions that test the detail of an imagined event, not only the fact of a remembered one.
examples.whyItMatters: A written plan can keep the test from becoming too narrow. You see the link when recall and future detail are checked side by side.

examples.title: Thread Promise Split
examples.scenario: Partner Margot thumbs "I can handle it" into the long text thread from a laundry room bench while unread replies keep sliding upward. Prospection gives her a calm evening and a neat answer. Serge reads the same request and writes a slower line: "I need to check the missing parts first." Her future-oriented picture runs on shine. His forecast has to name time, fatigue, and the reply that might otherwise get lost.
examples.whatToDo: Margot pauses before sending and copies Serge's slower line. She names the missing facts in the thread before she lets the smooth picture become a promise.
examples.whyItMatters: A vivid future can cool a relationship when it skips friction. Counting the omitted parts protects the person waiting for your reply.

examples.title: Aviary Reframe
examples.scenario: The Cambridge aviary latch sticks, and trainer Cassidy has to shoulder it twice before the western scrub jays settle. She says the birds "know the future." Nicola Clayton shakes her head. "Count what they can use, not what you hope it means." The 1998 work stays modest: what, where, and when are the testable parts.
examples.whatToDo: Cassidy rewrites her claim as a checklist of evidence. She counts item, place, and time before she says what the behavior can show.
examples.whyItMatters: The reframe travels to your forecasts. A lively story deserves the same check: what facts can it use, and what has it skipped?

questions.prompt: You are planning a hard conversation and can almost hear the other person's reply. What is your mind doing?
choices: It is turning a positive wish into confidence about a good result.
It is storing the plan as a memory so you can repeat it later.
It is simulating a possible future state before it arrives.
questions.explanation: Prospection is a preview of a possible future, not just optimism. The scene may be good, bad, or mixed, but it guides present behavior.

questions.prompt: A clinician sees a patient speak clearly yet struggle to plan beyond the next impulse. Which brain link best fits the case?
choices: Memory storage alone has failed, so the person cannot hold past facts.
Happiness has lost its single home, so the person cannot feel future joy.
Frontal control is weakened, so later goals no longer guide action well.
questions.explanation: The frontal-lobe link is planning, inhibition, and future-oriented control. Memory can feed forecasts, but frontal systems help steer behavior over time.

questions.prompt: At a Cavendish exhibit, a museum guide introduces Phineas Gage while pointing to a tamping iron. Which line stays closest to why the case matters here?
choices: He survived an 1848 tamping-iron accident that became a key case for frontal-lobe change.
He proved that happiness sits in one frontal area after a railroad injury exposed it.
He lost ordinary intelligence after a tool accident and could no longer answer questions.
questions.explanation: Gage anchors the link between frontal injury and changed control. The case does not locate happiness, and it is not a simple story of erased intelligence.

questions.prompt: In a clinic discussion, you hear someone say Patient H.M. became "unable to think" after surgery. What correction fits the case?
choices: His new episodic memory was deeply impaired, while some core intellectual abilities remained.
His future planning failed because his frontal lobes had been struck by a railroad tool.
His main loss was optimism, while ordinary learning and memory stayed mostly intact.
questions.explanation: Henry Molaison's 1953 surgery caused severe anterograde amnesia. The important split is damaged new episodic memory with partly spared intellect.

questions.prompt: A friend says future imagination cannot depend on memory because the event has not happened. Which reply matches prospection?
choices: Future scenes need only frontal control, since memory would trap the mind in the past.
Future scenes are separate from memory, since new events require new material.
Future scenes borrow stored detail, so memory problems can thin imagined events.
questions.explanation: A new scene still needs pieces: places, sequences, feelings, and context. That is why memory impairment can reduce future detail.

questions.prompt: During a Cambridge feeding trial, a researcher watches western scrub jays recover cached food. Which pattern would show more than a simple place habit?
choices: They return to the loudest cache site whenever the testing room changes.
They use what was stored, where it was stored, and when it was stored.
They choose the food with the strongest smell and ignore elapsed time.
questions.explanation: The scrub-jay work tested integrated what-where-when information. A smell cue or a familiar place alone would be closer to the reflex error.

questions.prompt: You discover that your forecast for a trip is biased. What should you conclude before throwing it away?
choices: A biased forecast is useless because planning needs a fully accurate picture.
A biased forecast can still help if it prepares action better than no forecast.
A useful forecast must be accurate because preparation proves the picture was true.
questions.explanation: Prospection can be adaptive while biased. A rough map may still help you pack, ask, save, or pause better than pure reaction.

questions.prompt: Before accepting a weekend plan, you can picture the drive, the room, and the easy mood so clearly that you stop checking it. What warning follows?
choices: Detail can come from fluency and borrowed pieces, so a clear scene may still omit key facts.
Detail usually proves realism because the mind would not add parts without evidence.
Detail mainly shows optimism because vivid plans are built around wanted outcomes.
questions.explanation: Vividness is not the same as accuracy. A fluent scene can feel convincing while it leaves out friction, timing, or other people's needs.

questions.prompt: You are about to trust a private forecast about a job change. Which next move follows the hard edge of prospection?
choices: Search your own feelings until the future image becomes stable enough to guide you.
Check the private image against outside facts and other people's experience.
Wait for the image to feel vivid, since strong detail is the best sign of fit.
questions.explanation: Self-knowledge helps, but it misses omitted details. Outside evidence gives the forecast a chance to be corrected before it steers a large choice.

reviewCards.front: What does prospection let your mind do before a future event arrives?
reviewCards.back: It lets you pre-experience a possible future by building a scene from memory, perception, and imagination. That preview then guides what you do now.

reviewCards.front: Why does Phineas Gage matter for a chapter about future planning?
reviewCards.back: After the 1848 tamping iron accident, Phineas Gage made planning look embodied. He could still speak while future-oriented control was badly changed.

reviewCards.front: What does Henry Molaison's case show about imagining detailed futures?
reviewCards.back: Henry Molaison's 1953 surgery damaged new episodic memory. His case shows why imagined personal events need remembered detail and sequence.

reviewCards.front: What did the scrub-jay caching work test?
reviewCards.back: At Cambridge, the work tested whether western scrub jays used what-where-when information. That pattern separates flexible memory from simple habit.

reviewCards.front: Why should a vivid forecast still be checked?
reviewCards.back: Vividness can come from fluent construction, not accuracy. A clear future scene may borrow detail from the wrong place and leave out facts that matter.

implementationPlan.title: Count the Missing Scene
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice using prospection without obeying it too fast. When a future scene feels clear, count one missing fact before you promise, buy, quit, or refuse. The move is simple: ask what the picture uses, then ask what it leaves out.

ifThenPlans.context: If a future picture feels smooth enough to make you hurry,
ifThenPlans.plan: then name one part the picture did not include before you act.

ifThenPlans.context: If someone presses you for a yes in the middle of a plan,
ifThenPlans.plan: then say, "I need to check what this picture leaves out before I promise."

ifThenPlans.context: If a bad memory starts writing every future version of a situation,
ifThenPlans.plan: then separate the old event from the next event and count one new fact.

ifThenPlans.context: If a forecast feels vivid because you want relief,
ifThenPlans.plan: then ask what evidence outside your head could correct it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For the next day, count each time a clear future scene pushes you toward a quick yes or no. Mark whether it skipped time, friction, or another person.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: This week, swap one instant promise for a counted pause. For the first half, answer as usual; for the second half, count one missing fact before replying and compare the strain.

memorableLines.text: A clear inner movie can still be a bad map.
memorableLines.why: It keeps the chapter's warning portable and visual.

memorableLines.text: Foresight needs brakes as much as it needs pictures.
memorableLines.why: It turns skepticism into a practical part of planning.

memorableLines.text: A forecast earns trust when the world gets a vote.
memorableLines.why: It names the outside check that makes prospection useful.

chapters.title: Subjectivity
chapters.hook: How can a survey room go quiet after every form is turned in, yet still change the answer?
chapters.counterintuition: Why does your own happiness need a careful measuring plan? The feeling is private, but the report shifts when memory, wording, and the last few minutes get a vote.
chapters.tryThisNow: During your first drink tomorrow, take ten minutes to write one morning episode and one feeling word where you already keep notes.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Your happiness report is not a perfect meter; it is the best direct clue when asked near the feeling, worded carefully, and checked across many lives.

breakdown.fastRead: Lucie has just finished a day log, and the survey room looks cleaner than her memory feels. One page asks for the day in episodes: commute, work, lunch, ride home. A broad life question would let her tell one polished story. The Day Reconstruction Method makes her slow down and mark what each part felt like. Feelings need witnesses, not mind readers. The witness is still Lucie, because no one else can feel from inside her skull. But the form asks close enough to the day that the answer has less time to become a speech.
breakdown.deepRead:
Miles pulls his hand out of the cold water and knows, for one second, that the shorter trial should win. Then the ending starts talking. The longer trial had extra pain, but it eased near the finish, and his memory likes that gentler exit.

That is the mechanism Gilbert wants you to see. Experienced utility means the moment-by-moment feeling while life is happening. Remembered utility means the later judgment you carry away. They often travel together, but they are not the same passenger. Memory edits pain; endings hold the pen.

Daniel Kahneman's cold-water work makes the split hard to ignore. A person can prefer to repeat the longer painful trial when its final moments are less unpleasant. That does not mean the body enjoyed more cold water. It means the later story used the ending as a shortcut.

This is why happiness research cannot rely only on your grand verdict about life. It also cannot throw your report away. Ask in ways that catch the feeling before memory has cleaned it up. Ask about episodes. Ask many people. Watch how wording changes the answer. A private feeling can still leave public evidence when researchers build the question with care.
breakdown.fullRead:
Leon is halfway through a survey when a dating question changes the whole room. He has been answering about life in general. Then the form asks about dating, and suddenly Saturday night has a louder voice than rent, sleep, work, or the friend he forgot to call.

Fritz Strack, Leonard Martin, and Norbert Schwarz showed why this matters. When dating frequency came first, the link between dating and life satisfaction looked stronger. The people were not lying. A clear question can still steer attention. Bad questions can make honest answers wobble.

That is the hard part of subjective happiness measurement. Subjective means first-person: the feeling belongs to the person having it. Measurement means you still try to learn from it without pretending you own a perfect meter. If you ask one person one broad question, you get noise. If you ask many people, close to lived episodes, with careful wording, the noise starts to show a pattern.

This protects you from two lazy answers. The first says happiness is too private for science, so every report is just a mood in costume. The second says a survey answer is pure truth, as if income, health, facial expression, or one checkbox could settle the matter. Neither answer works. You need the person's report, and you need guardrails around it.

Those guardrails are plain. Ask near the experience when you can. Break a day into scenes instead of asking for a single life headline. Compare many reports rather than worship one. Notice question order. Separate what felt good while it happened from what memory later praised.

This also matters at home. If you ask yourself, "Was this week good?" after a brutal Friday, Friday may swallow the week. If you ask, "Which parts of Thursday actually felt okay?" you may recover the walk, the quiet lunch, or the message you meant to send before the day scattered. You are not becoming a machine. You are giving your own answer less room to drift.

The cost shows up when a big story spends real money. A person who remembers only the relaxed final night of a trip may book another one while the rent account is already thin. The feeling report needs the whole set of episodes, not only the scene memory kept shiny.

Here is where the idea stops working: it cannot tell you what someone else secretly feels when that person is unsafe, coached, ashamed, or punished for the answer. A worker who fears losing a job may report calm. A teenager may say "fine" because the kitchen is listening. Careful self-report is the best direct clue to happiness, not a magic window into a guarded mind.

examples.title: Episode Page
examples.scenario: Lucie's pencil pauses above the wide life-satisfaction line, ready to make yesterday sound fine. On the next page, the Day Reconstruction Method asks for episodes instead. Among 909 employed women, her commute, desk work, lunch, and ride home no longer collapse into one tidy answer.
examples.whatToDo: Lucie stops forcing a single verdict. She writes the day in pieces, then marks how each piece felt before a later story can smooth the edges.
examples.whyItMatters: The same life can look different when you ask about lived episodes. That makes self-report more useful without pretending it is perfect.

examples.title: Ending Mistake
examples.scenario: Participant Miles lowers his hand in the cold-water lab toward the basin during the repeat-choice round before the mistake catches up with him. The 90 seconds ended less harshly than the 60 seconds, so his mind calls it better. Then he sees the extra half minute he is about to choose.
examples.whatToDo: Miles separates the ending from the whole trial. He names the pull of the last moments before he treats his remembered preference as total pain.
examples.whyItMatters: A remembered ending can overrule the full experience. Catching that slip keeps one polished memory from choosing the worse repeat.

examples.title: Saturday First
examples.scenario: Leon's pencil is moving across the survey when the dating question appears first. In the setup from Fritz Strack, Leonard Martin, and Norbert Schwarz, Saturday night crowds into his head. He thinks about unanswered texts, then judges his whole life through that suddenly bright doorway.
examples.whatToDo: Leon notices which memory the first question made easy to reach. He answers, but he treats that answer as shaped by the order of the form.
examples.whyItMatters: The report is still meaningful. The warning is that a clear question can change which evidence a person uses to answer the next one.

examples.title: Verdict Crossed Out
examples.scenario: The single life score is already crossed out on the research table before the Day Reconstruction Method form is copied. Survey designer Marguerite has not asked anyone to answer yet. She budgets attention for yesterday's episodes, not a grand speech, so 909 employed women can report feelings without carrying a full diary.
examples.whatToDo: Marguerite gives the scarce space to episodes and feelings. She removes the broad verdict that would invite a polished life story.
examples.whyItMatters: Good measurement starts before the answer. The form can either help memory find concrete scenes or push it toward a vague public story.

examples.title: More Cold
examples.scenario: Every choice on the repeat form means more cold water. Iris must choose between the 60 seconds that stayed sharp to the end and the 90 seconds that added time but eased off. Neither line promises comfort; the peak-end rule only gives one a kinder last note.
examples.whatToDo: Iris names both costs before she circles a line. She does not let the gentler ending masquerade as a smaller total dose of discomfort.
examples.whyItMatters: The dilemma makes the peak-end rule visible. Memory can prefer a story with a better finish while the body endured more.

examples.title: No Perfect Meter
examples.scenario: "They just say what sounds good," Levi says on the stairwell landing, and Lucas stops with the forms under his arm. "Daniel Kahneman still asks," Lucas says. "So use only income?" Levi shakes his head. "No. Ask closer, ask cleaner, and ask enough people that one noisy answer is not the whole case."
examples.whatToDo: Lucas keeps the self-reports, but he changes the standard. He looks for better timing, cleaner wording, and patterns across many answers.
examples.whyItMatters: The right response to noisy reports is discipline, not surrender. Outside signs can help, but they cannot feel happiness for the person.

questions.prompt: You see a coworker smiling after a raise and want to know if they are happy. What should you remember?
choices: Income and facial signs can settle happiness when the signs point the same way.
A person's felt happiness is directly available only from that person's own experience.
Health and behavior are better measures than reports because they are outside the mind.
questions.explanation: The fact says happiness is a private felt state. Outside signs may hint at it, but they do not directly equal the feeling.

questions.prompt: A researcher worries that one survey answer is noisy but still wants the signal. What is the best next move?
choices: Discard reports because a biased answer cannot carry any useful signal.
Replace reports with income data because outside numbers avoid all bias.
Collect many careful reports because shared patterns can emerge from noisy answers.
questions.explanation: Imperfect reports can still be useful when gathered carefully and combined. The common error is throwing away any report that has bias.

questions.prompt: A survey asks you to rebuild yesterday as a set of episodes and rate feelings during each part. What method does that match?
choices: It matches a brain scan because it reads happiness without asking for words.
It matches a therapy exercise because it aims to treat distress after the fact.
It matches the Day Reconstruction Method because it uses episodes from the prior day.
questions.explanation: The Day Reconstruction Method is structured self-report about yesterday's episodes. It is not a neural measure or a treatment plan.

questions.prompt: A manager asks about commute stress before asking workers how satisfied they are with the job. What risk should the manager notice?
choices: The first question can make commute stress unusually easy to use in the next judgment.
The first question is harmless as long as the wording is clear and polite.
The first question proves commute stress causes the whole satisfaction score.
questions.explanation: Question order can steer attention before the next answer. Clear wording does not remove that context effect, and the order alone does not prove cause.

questions.prompt: A survey finds a stronger link between dating frequency and life satisfaction when dating is asked first. What should you infer?
choices: Dating must be the main cause of life satisfaction for the people answering.
The link would stay the same if the dating question came after life satisfaction.
The first question made dating more available when people judged overall happiness.
questions.explanation: The dating-order effect is about attention and judgment context. It does not show that dating causes overall happiness.

questions.prompt: You remember a hard trip as fine because the last hour went well, even though most of the trip felt tense. Which distinction explains the mismatch?
choices: Remembered utility can differ from moment-by-moment experience because memory weights endings.
Remembered utility usually adds each part with the same weight in the later judgment.
Experienced utility is just the later story you tell after the event is over.
questions.explanation: Experienced utility names what felt true while it happened. Remembered utility names the later judgment, which can overweight peaks and endings.

questions.prompt: A participant faces two cold-water trials and chooses the longer one after it ends more gently. What best explains that choice?
choices: The longer trial must have contained less discomfort overall than the shorter trial.
The milder ending shaped the later evaluation more than total duration did.
The participant must have ignored the ending and summed every second evenly.
questions.explanation: The longer trial added discomfort, but the less unpleasant ending changed the memory of it. That is why the choice is revealing.

questions.prompt: A team wants to make a general claim about what improves daily mood. What should they avoid?
choices: Using one honest answer as enough evidence for a broad rule.
Looking for stable tendencies across many repeated reports.
Checking whether wording or mood may have shaped a response.
questions.explanation: One honest answer can still be shaped by mood, wording, or memory. Larger samples help separate pattern from noise.

questions.prompt: A colleague says the Day Reconstruction Method was designed mainly as therapy for distress. Which correction fits the source?
choices: It was built to replace all surveys with brain data about happiness.
It was published as a survey approach to experienced well-being.
It was created to make broad life stories more polished and public.
questions.explanation: The source frames the Day Reconstruction Method as a survey method for experienced well-being. It was not therapy or a brain measure.

reviewCards.front: What does subjective happiness measurement try to do without pretending to own a perfect meter?
reviewCards.back: It asks people what they feel, then improves the evidence through timing, wording, repeated reports, and comparison across many people.

reviewCards.front: How does the 2004 Science Day Reconstruction Method make a happiness report more concrete?
reviewCards.back: It asks 909 employed women to rebuild the previous day as episodes and rate feelings in those parts, instead of giving one broad life verdict.

reviewCards.front: Why did the dating-order effect matter for life satisfaction reports?
reviewCards.back: Fritz Strack, Leonard Martin, and Norbert Schwarz showed that when dating came first, it became easier to use in the next answer.

reviewCards.front: What does the cold-water choice reveal about experienced and remembered utility?
reviewCards.back: Moment-by-moment pain and later judgment can split. A gentler ending can make 90 seconds of cold water seem better than 60 seconds afterward.

reviewCards.front: Why is one honest happiness answer not enough for a general rule?
reviewCards.back: Honesty does not remove mood, wording, memory, or sampling error. Many careful reports make stable patterns easier to see.

reviewCards.front: Recall Prospection (Ch 1): name one concrete moment here where it actually bites.
reviewCards.back: Miles shows it in the cold-water lab: his mind previews a repeat trial from the remembered ending, not from the full pain he just lived.

implementationPlan.title: Mark the Feeling Close
implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice catching your happiness report before it becomes a speech. Ask about a concrete episode, mark what was happening around it, and treat the answer as evidence rather than a final verdict. The skill is not to distrust yourself; it is to ask yourself in a cleaner way.

ifThenPlans.context: If you catch yourself calling the whole day good or bad
ifThenPlans.plan: If one label flattens the day, then mark the feeling close: borrow the Day Reconstruction Method move used with 909 employed women and split the day into episodes.

ifThenPlans.context: If a memory feels better mainly because it ended well
ifThenPlans.plan: If the ending is doing all the talking, then mark the feeling close: compare the full 60 seconds or 90 seconds with the final moments the peak-end rule favors.

ifThenPlans.context: If the first question makes one topic feel unusually important
ifThenPlans.plan: If one topic starts to feel like the whole answer, then mark the feeling close: use Fritz Strack, Leonard Martin, and Norbert Schwarz's warning and name what the first question made loud.

ifThenPlans.context: If you want to read someone else's mood
ifThenPlans.plan: If pay, health, or a smile seems like proof, then mark the feeling close: ask for the person's report before you trust the sign.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: During your next commute or first coffee, write one sentence where you already keep notes: what is happening right now, and what does it feel like?
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: This week, teach one person why a happiness report is useful but noisy. Use Lucie's episode page or Miles's cold-water ending as your example.
